endings.user: Compact. I know I won't carry anything big around.
endings.moshi: That's honest and smart. The best camera is the one you actually bring with you.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You'll be fine with a plan. Do you want to focus on posed group shots, or candid moments as the party happens?

endings.user: Posed first, then candid once people relax.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why do my photos of the moon always come out as a blurry white dot?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The moon is much brighter than the night sky, so the camera overexposes it. Lowering the exposure a lot usually brings back the detail.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm just using my phone.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Tap on the moon, then slide the brightness down until you see the craters. Zoom only as far as the phone's optical zoom goes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And it's always / a bit shaky too.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Rest the phone on something solid, or use a small tripod. A two second timer stops your finger from shaking it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Cool, I'll try tonight. It's almost full.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect timing. Try shooting it right after it rises, when it looks bigger near the horizon.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What does aperture actually mean? I keep reading it and nodding.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's the size of the opening in the lens that lets light in. A wide opening means more light and a blurrier background.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And the numbers, like f two?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Confusingly, smaller numbers mean a wider opening. So f two gives a soft background, and f eleven keeps everything sharp.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So for a portrait I'd want / the small number?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. For a landscape where you want the whole scene sharp, go with a bigger number like f eight.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Got it. That makes way more sense now.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm going on safari next month. What lens should I bring?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A telephoto zoom is the key one, something that reaches at least three hundred millimeters. Animals are often far away.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Those are heavy, right?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They can be. Many safari vehicles have something to rest it on, and a small bean bag makes a great steady support.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I bring / a second camera body or is that overkill?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If you have one, it's handy. Changing lenses in dusty air can get dirt on the sensor, so two bodies saves a lot of hassle.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I only have one. I'll just be careful then.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That works. Change lenses inside the vehicle with the camera pointing down, and pack extra batteries and memory cards.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm a retired teacher and I just bought my first camera. I want to photograph birds in my garden.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lovely hobby. A bird feeder near a window gives you a steady stream of subjects without scaring them off.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They fly off as soon as / I open the back door.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Shoot from inside through an open window, or sit very still outside for ten minutes. Birds get used to a quiet person surprisingly fast.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And what setting should I use? They move so quickly.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Use a fast shutter speed, around one thousandth of a second, and burst mode. Then keep the sharpest shot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Burst mode is the one that clicks a lot?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's the one. Hold the button down and it takes several photos per second.
